prompt.context: Your friend, Anne, works as a dentist at a private practice. The owner of that practice, Dr. D, has owned the practice for 20 years and has decided that he is finally ready to retire. After searching for years for a replacement, he believes Anne is the right person to take over the practice and has offered to sell it to her. Anne truly enjoys her job; though she isn't sure if she would enjoy actually owning and managing the business.
prompt.question: She wants your help figuring out whether or not she should purchase the practice.

clarifying_info.q: What are the current financials of the practice?
clarifying_info.a: After paying all expenses (including Anne's $100K salary), the practice generates a profit of $150K per year, which is taken as income by Dr. D.

clarifying_info.q: How much is Dr. D asking for the practice?
clarifying_info.a: Dr. D has offered to sell the practice to Anne for $1M.

clarifying_info.q: How much time does Anne spend on patient care vs. admin work?
clarifying_info.a: Anne currently works for 8 hours a day including 2 hours of administrative work. Dr. D sees patients for 2 hours a day.

clarifying_info.q: Can Anne offload her administrative tasks?
clarifying_info.a: Assume Anne can offload all her administrative tasks by hiring a dental technician for a salary of $50K.
For our purposes, assume the market will stay as-is.

framework: Profitability: Revenue (price points, patient volume, patient retention risk) and Costs (fixed: dental technicians, lease; variable: patient acquisition, equipment, medication)
Dental Market Dynamics: number of competitors in the area, macroeconomic trends, new technologies and regulations
Fit: Anne's skills and desire to run a private practice, and the acquisition price relative to value

questions.prompt: What are the main drivers of profitability for the practice, and what are the greatest risks?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify revenue drivers (price, patient volume) and cost drivers (fixed: staff/lease; variable: equipment/supplies). The most critical risk is patient attrition when Dr. D retires — patients may have loyalty to Dr. D personally. Mitigation ideas: have Dr. D gradually wind down patient work, have Dr. D send a letter endorsing Anne to his patients, offer loyalty discounts or gestures to retain existing patients.

questions.prompt: Anne already has a full patient load. Dr. D sees patients 2 hours/day on top of Anne's 8-hour day. How does this affect staffing, and what happens to annual profits?
questions.guidance: Anne is at capacity, so she cannot absorb Dr. D's patient hours. She would need to hire help. If she offloads her 2 hours of daily admin to a dental technician at $50K/year, she frees up time for patient care. This replaces Anne's $100K salary cost with a $50K technician salary, saving $50K, which flows to profit.

math.setup: Original profit (after Anne's $100K salary) = $150K. Replace Anne's salary with dental technician salary of $50K. Net saving = $100K - $50K = $50K added to profit.

questions.prompt: Using a discount rate of 10% and assuming profits continue in perpetuity, calculate the NPV of purchasing the practice versus not purchasing it. What does this tell Anne?
questions.guidance: Use perpetuity formula (Value = Cash Flow / Discount Rate). Compare NPV of buying to NPV of staying as employee. Both options yield NPV of $1M, so Anne is financially indifferent. The decision should hinge on non-financial factors such as fit and personal preference.

math.setup: Perpetuity value = Annual profit / Discount rate. NPV of buying = Practice value - Purchase price. NPV of not buying = PV of Anne's salary as employee in perpetuity.
steps: Both options yield NPV = $1M → Anne is financially indifferent
math.answer: NPV of both options = $1M; Anne is indifferent on financial grounds alone

questions.prompt: What skills would someone need to successfully run a private dental practice?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm in a structured way, for example grouping by: Dental Skills (clinical expertise, continuing education), Administrative Skills (scheduling, billing, insurance), Human Resources Skills (hiring, managing staff, payroll), and Other (marketing/patient acquisition, financial management, legal/compliance).

brainstorming.prompt: What types of skills do you think someone would need to run a private practice?

categories.name: Dental Skills
ideas: Knowledge of current dental procedures and technologies

recommendation: Do not purchase the practice at this time
Financially, both paths (buy vs. stay as employee) yield an NPV of $1M, so there is no financial advantage to buying
Anne has indicated she likely does not enjoy managing a business, and the fit dimension argues against purchasing
risks: Patient attrition when Dr. D retires could reduce practice value
Anne may struggle with the management and HR demands of ownership
Market conditions or competition could deteriorate
next_steps: Understand what Dr. D will do with the practice if Anne declines — will she keep her job and salary?
Explore whether Anne's salary would remain at $100K under new ownership
If Anne reconsiders, negotiate a lower purchase price or a transitional arrangement where Dr. D stays part-time to retain patients
